# Max-product inference in logarithmic form

Consider a factorized nonnegative function

$$
F(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\prod_{a=1}^M\phi_a(x_{N(a)}).
$$

The most probable explanation is

$$
x^*\in\arg\max_x F(x).
$$

Writing $T_a=\log\phi_a$ turns products into sums:

$$
x^*\in\arg\max_x\sum_aT_a(x_{N(a)}).
$$

This is a tensor contraction over the max-plus, or tropical, semiring.

::: {#def-tropical-semiring .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: max-plus semiring

The max-plus semiring is

$$
\mathbb T=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\},
\qquad
a\oplus b=\max(a,b),
\qquad
a\otimes b=a+b.
$$

Its additive identity is $-\infty$ and its multiplicative identity is $0$.
:::

Hard constraints are represented by tensors with value $0$ on allowed assignments and $-\infty$ on forbidden assignments. For syndrome decoding, a check factor is

$$
T_a(e_{N(a)})=
\begin{cases}
0,&\bigoplus_{i\in N(a)}e_i=s_a,\\
-\infty,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

# Tensor contraction

In ordinary arithmetic, eliminating a variable sums over its values. In max-plus arithmetic, elimination maximizes:

$$
B(y)=\bigoplus_x A(x,y)=\max_xA(x,y).
$$

Combining factors uses tropical multiplication, which is ordinary addition. A complete contraction therefore returns the maximum log weight of any configuration. This is the same algebraic principle used to compute exact ground states of discrete spin models [@liu2021tropical].

::: {#thm-tropical-map .callout-important icon="false"}
## Theorem: tropical contraction computes MAP value

If every configuration weight factorizes as $F(x)=\prod_a\phi_a(x_{N(a)})$, then contracting the log-factor network over $(\max,+)$ returns

$$
\max_x\log F(x)=\log\max_xF(x).
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Proof

Distributivity of addition over maximum permits variables to be eliminated in any valid contraction order:

$$
\max_x\sum_a\log\phi_a(x_{N(a)})
=\log\max_x\prod_a\phi_a(x_{N(a)}).
$$

Tensor contraction is repeated application of these two semiring operations.
:::

# Recovering an optimizing configuration

A scalar contraction gives only the optimal value. To recover $x^*$, store an argmax table whenever a variable or group of variables is eliminated.

::: {#def-tropical-backpointer .callout-note icon="false"}
## Definition: backpointer

For a reduction

$$
B(y)=\max_xA(x,y),
$$

a backpointer is a choice

$$
b(y)\in\arg\max_xA(x,y).
$$
:::

After the forward contraction, traverse the contraction tree in reverse. Values already assigned to the surviving indices select a row of each backpointer table, which recovers the eliminated indices. Ties require a deterministic convention if one optimizer is desired. To count optimizers as well, augment each tropical value with a multiplicity and add multiplicities on ties [@liu2021tropical].

# Complexity and contraction width

The dominant cost is the largest intermediate tensor. For variables of domain size $q$, an elimination order of induced width $w$ requires time and memory exponential in $w$ (up to polynomial factors):

$$
\operatorname{cost}\sim\operatorname{poly}(n)q^{w+1}.
$$

The minimum possible induced width is characterized by the treewidth of the primal interaction graph. Bounded degree does not imply bounded treewidth: a sparse expander has linear treewidth, while an $L\times L$ grid has treewidth $\Theta(L)$. Thus a two-dimensional code with $n\asymp L^2$ typically leads to a subexponential but still superpolynomial exact contraction, roughly $\exp[O(\sqrt n)]$.

Heuristic contraction-order optimizers can greatly improve constants but do not change this worst-case dependence. Approximate boundary-MPS contraction replaces exact intermediate tensors by controlled low-rank approximations; this underlies tensor-network decoders for surface codes [@bravyi2014efficient].

# Physical MAP is not degenerate quantum ML

For a syndrome $s$, tropical contraction of physical-error factors computes

$$
\max_{E:s(E)=s}\Pr(E),
$$

the probability of the most likely representative. A degenerate quantum decoder instead needs

$$
\max_L\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}\Pr(E_sLS).
$$

The inner operation here is a **sum**, not a maximum. Replacing it by max-plus discards the entropy of each stabilizer coset.

::: {#lem-tropical-degeneracy-limit .callout-important icon="false"}
## Lemma: max-plus cannot perform the coset sum

In general,

$$
\max_{S\in\mathcal S}\Pr(E_sLS)
\ne
\sum_{S\in\mathcal S}\Pr(E_sLS),
$$

and the logical coset maximizing the left-hand quantity need not maximize the right-hand quantity.
:::

For example, one coset containing a representative of probability $0.4$ beats another whose largest representative has probability $0.3$ under max-product. But if the second coset has two representatives of probability $0.3$, its total probability is $0.6$ and it is preferred by degenerate ML.

Coset-aware decoding therefore requires ordinary sum-product contraction, log-sum-exp arithmetic, or an augmented algebra that retains the necessary partition sums. Tropical contraction remains exact and useful when the target is a MAP configuration, a minimum-energy representative, or a zero-temperature limit.

# Comparison

| Method | Primary output | Exact objective | Dominant cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| BP | approximate marginals | exact on trees | iterations $\times$ graph edges |
| BP+OSD | short list of valid representatives | heuristic list search | elimination plus list size |
| Tropical TN | MAP value and representative | max-product objective | exponential in contraction width |
| Sum-product TN | partition or coset probability | marginal/coset sum | exponential in contraction width |

: Decoder objectives should be compared before runtime or threshold numbers.

# Implementation invariants

A correct implementation should preserve

- $-\infty$ for forbidden configurations;
- a stable tie policy for backpointers;
- an explicit map from tensor indices to error variables;
- enough backpointer metadata to invert every reduction;
- a separately verified syndrome for the recovered assignment; and
- a distinction between representative MAP and logical-coset ML in all reported results.
